newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thousands of miners leave Bonn, protests go on.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of miners leave Bonn, protests go on.

text.p: Thousands of German coal miners protesting in Bonn against subsidy cuts headed home on Tuesday, following an appeal from their union leader to wait for the outcome of crisis talks Chancellor Kohl postponed to Thursday.

After thousands of angry pit workers virtually besieged the government quarter in Bonn and blockaded a major highway, Kohl cancelled talks set for Tuesday because of what officials described as "an atmosphere of intimidation".

Incensed by the postponement, hundreds of miners forced their way through a police barricade into an exclusion zone shouting: "We're going to the chancellery!". The atmosphere stayed tense and teetered on the brink of violence.
The confrontation with the miners is perhaps the most dramatic sign yet of growing discontent with an apparently endless series of welfare cuts, budget savings and job losses.
In a passionate speech the leader of the IG Bergbau miners' union, Hans Berger, appealed to the miners to go home for the time being and wait for the outcome of Thursday's talks.
Berger said Bonn was to blame for stoking up the protests, telling reporters: "The lack of readiness to compromise is likely to be seen as a provocation."
"Those who are prepared to meet us to reach a reasonable solution should never be made to feel they're under pressure," Berger told a rally in Bonn.
"Don't let them steal the arguments," he urged them. "Protest in your regions and if no compromise is reached, we are ready to come back!"
Some pit workers were not convinced. Booing and jeering, they shouted "lier" at him and chanted "Kohl must resign".
Most of the 13,000 or so demonstrators from Germany's ailing steel-and-coal heartland and the Saar state on the French border began to disperse.
A few stayed behind to wait for 9,000 miners who held rallies all day in Saar and were heading to Bonn. Berger said he would hold another rally to explain the situation to them.
A small hard core, who accused Berger of betraying them by agreeing to meet Kohl for talks, said they were not budging until they had a "reasonalbe offer".

"We're staying here until Thursday when a decision is made," said miner Ruediger Heinze, 36, from the pit town of Dinslaken in the Ruhr. "We're only going home when we get a straight answer from Bonn on how much money we're getting."
Heinze sat outside the Chancellery with a small group of miners all wrapped up in blankets.

Earlier Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl told reporters on the fringe of a cabinet meeting that "reasonable talks cannot be held in such a tense atmosphere". He said Kohl would meet Berger on condition the miners ended their protest.

The government gave no sign that it was prepared to give ground to the miners, who stopped work in Germany's 18 pits on Friday after Bonn said it would cut subsidies to 3.8 billion marks by 2005 instead of the promised 6.5 billion.
Currently Bonn pays over nine billion marks a year to compensate users for a domestic coal price which is over three times the world market price.
IG Bergbau says the government plans will force 10 pits to close by 2005, make 50,000 miners redundant and cause a further 70,000 related job losses in already depressed areas.
Economics Minister Guenther Rexrodt of the FDP said there was scant room to compromise when each mining job cost the government 130,000 marks ($76,200) a year.

"Our offer means we are providing more than 50 billion marks for the mining sector over nine years," he told German Radio. "Coal subsidies have been declining for many decades, and it was well known that there would be a cut in 1997 of the order that has been proposed."
